Zero-shot performance still requires supervised adaptation on medical source datasets, including pixel masks for segmentation training. Few-shot adaptation additionally assumes access to labeled target abnormalities, limiting applicability when only normal images or image-level labels are available.

The unseen-modality/anatomy evaluation is not fully established by leave-one-dataset-out testing. RESC and OCT17 both contain retinal OCT images, and the paper does not clarify whether both are excluded from training when either is tested.

Validation is restricted to six public datasets, with segmentation assessed on only three. No explicit site-held-out or prospective clinical evaluation, scanner/protocol robustness testing, or demographic subgroup analysis is reported, limiting claims of universal medical generalization.

For slice-based datasets, patient- or volume-level separation between labeled training pools and test samples is not explicitly documented. Consequently, leakage through correlated slices cannot be ruled out, and image counts do not establish the number of independent patients evaluated.

Few-shot results lack reported variability across independently sampled support sets and training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The normal/abnormal composition of the K-shot samples is also unspecified, making stability with only 2–16 images difficult to assess.

Evaluation relies exclusively on image- and pixel-level AUROC. Precision-recall performance, clinically relevant sensitivity/specificity operating points, calibration, segmentation overlap, and lesion-level detection metrics are absent; high pixel-AUROC alone does not establish accurate lesion delineation.

Processing volumes and whole-slide images as resized 2D slices or patches omits broader anatomical context. The 240-pixel input resolution and coarse ViT patch grid may lose subtle abnormalities or fine boundaries, which bilinear upsampling cannot recover.

Comparisons with WinCLIP and normal-only baselines are not supervision-matched: MVFA receives abnormal labels and, for segmentation, pixel annotations that these methods do not use. Those performance differences therefore cannot be attributed solely to the adapter architecture.

The loss formulation assumes pixel-level masks, but HIS, ChestXray, and OCT17 provide only image-level labels. How segmentation losses and dual-adapter branches are handled for these partially annotated training datasets is not specified.

The ablations do not establish that language alignment is necessary. Without a parameter-matched visual-only adapter trained using the same labels, improvements cannot be cleanly distinguished from ordinary supervised feature adaptation and multi-level supervision.

Evidence for substantial benefits from multi-level score ensembling is limited: in the K=4 ablation, average gains over the strongest individual level are only 0.13 percentage points for classification and 0.05 for segmentation. Their statistical reliability and practical value relative to added complexity are not established.

Residual ratios, loss weights, prompt templates, and branch-fusion weights are adopted without sensitivity analysis. In particular, equal-weight fusion combines softmax scores and cosine distances with different numerical ranges without demonstrated calibration.

The lightweight claim lacks end-to-end computational evidence. The system retains a CLIP ViT-L/14 backbone and uses multi-level nearest-neighbor retrieval in few-shot mode, but parameter counts, inference latency, peak memory, training time, and memory-bank scaling are not quantified.

The few-shot experiments do not explicitly separate supported pathology types from unseen anomaly subtypes. Sensitivity to genuinely novel diseases, and possible specialization toward the few annotated abnormalities, therefore remain unmeasured.

Average improvements obscure substantial domain-specific variation: much of the K=4 classification gain over April-GAN comes from LiverCT, while zero-shot BrainMRI segmentation is worse at 90.27% versus 91.79% AUROC. Systematic error analysis by pathology, lesion size, and false-positive or false-negative category is missing.
